lines.trans: Not one chipped cup, zero blown fuses, and twenty-four happy neighbours.
You are smiling, Tariq! I saw it clearly under the lamp!
Must be a trick of the frosted glass, Nour.
Nour, before you close the big paper reservation book tonight...
Is everything all right in Room Four, Suad? Did the buzzer ring twice again?
I have grown quite fond of that double ring—is Room Four free next week?
Wait—you want to extend your stay with us, Suad?!
Two more weeks, if you will have me—and I will play every Friday for tea!
Room Four belongs to you as long as you want it, madam.
Written in pencil right here! Salma and Mazen will be thrilled!
Oh, by the way, the postman slipped a thick foreign postcard into the gate box.
Evening mail on a Friday? Let us take it to the front desk!

meanings.note: With two pronunciations in context: walla ('or' in choice questions: عالشارع ولا عالساحة؟) and wala ('not even / nor': ولا خدش 'not a single scratch', ولا يهمك 'do not worry at all').

examples.trans: Is the window facing the street or the courtyard?
Not a single drop of water on the table!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: فناجين.

examples.trans: I set two teacups on the tray.
This is my favourite coffee cup.

meanings.note: Spoken Arabic word for a chipped or hairline-cracked cup or plate.

examples.trans: We used the word مشروخ.
This is another مشروخ.

meanings.note: Loanword from English 'fuse'; when one blows, people say الفيوز ضرب.

examples.trans: I changed the fuse and the light came back.
The fuse box is next to the door.

meanings.note: Literally 'burnt', used in Arabic for a blown electrical fuse or lightbulb.

examples.trans: We used the word محروق.
This is another محروق.

meanings.note: Numeral 'four'; short form أربع (arba') directly before a plural noun (أربع طاولات 'four tables').

examples.trans: Room four is arriving today.
Four tables and eight chairs in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Numeral 'twenty' (followed by a singular noun in Arabic: عشرين دقيقة 'twenty minutes').

examples.trans: We need twenty eggs for breakfast.
The ring's width is twenty millimetres.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: جيران.

examples.trans: All the neighbours on the street are kind.
Good morning, dear neighbour.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: مبسوطة, plural: مبسوطين).

examples.trans: We are very glad that you liked the courtyard.
The guests left happy from breakfast.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian pronoun 'you' when addressing one man.

examples.trans: Did you plant these herbs yourself?
Did you plan this entire meeting?

meanings.note: Levantine progressive marker placed before a present-tense verb to show action happening right now.

examples.trans: The water is flowing inside the pipe right now!

examples.text: كنت عم بدور على دفتري هلا.
examples.trans: I was just looking for my notebook.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (ببتسم, بيبتسم).

examples.trans: Smile when the bell rings!
He smiled when he saw his brother.

meanings.note: Placed directly before a name or title when addressing someone in Arabic (يا نور 'Nour!', يا أستاذ 'sir!') and in exclamations (يا سلام! 'wonderful!').

examples.trans: Good morning, Tariq!
Oh, how lovely the sun is after the rain!

meanings.note: Male given name of the veteran handyman.

examples.trans: We used the word طارق.
This is another طارق.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb for 'to see, look, check' (بشوف / شاف).

examples.trans: Look inside the suitcase, Nour!
I will see you tomorrow at breakfast.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: I can hear you clearly on the phone now.
He explained the idea with complete clarity.

meanings.note: Used both before a noun ('under, beneath') and standalone ('downstairs').

examples.trans: Let us bring it downstairs into the light.
The wide desk is under the window.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: لمبات.

examples.trans: I fitted a new bulb in the attic bathroom.
The white lightbulb is bright.

meanings.note: Means 'certainly, definitely' or 'must be' (إنتي أكيد نور 'you must be Nour').

examples.trans: Hello! You must be Nour.

examples.text: أكيد صاحبه رح يدور عليه قريبا.
examples.trans: Surely its owner will look for it soon.

meanings.note: Feminine Arabic noun meaning 'trick' or 'illusion'.

examples.trans: We used the word خدعة.
This is another خدعة.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition meaning 'from', 'of', or 'than' after comparatives.

examples.trans: I am Salma from the kitchen.
Breakfast is from seven-thirty to ten.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian form of زجاج ('glass').

examples.trans: Look at the courtyard through the window glass.
We wiped the glass this morning until it shone.

meanings.note: Masculine Arabic word meaning 'frosted' or 'sandblasted' glass.

examples.trans: We used the word مصنفر.
This is another مصنفر.

meanings.note: Appears in صباح النور ('morning of light', the standard reply to صباح الخير) and نور الشمس ('sunlight').

examples.trans: Good morning and welcome!
We read the card in the sunlight.

meanings.note: Means 'before' (قبل الفطور) and with a time span 'ago' (قبل ساعة 'an hour ago', قبل شوي 'just now').

examples.text: علمت بيانو هون قبل خمسة وعشرين سنة.
examples.trans: I taught piano here twenty-five years ago.
Drink your coffee before the rush.

meanings.note: Negates verbs and في (ما بعرف 'I don't know', ما في 'there isn't'), and links conjunctions like قبل ما ('before') and بعد ما ('after').

examples.trans: Paper does not lose room names.
Have tea before you head out.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بسكر, بيسكر).

examples.trans: He said thank you and hung up!
Did you shut off the main water valve?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: دفاتر.

examples.trans: We wrote the name in the booking ledger.
I forgot my leather notebook on the table.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: حجوزات.

examples.trans: I have a booking for a double room.
I read the booking ledger in the morning.

meanings.note: Masculine word formed from ورق ('paper'), meaning 'made of paper'.

examples.trans: We used the word ورقي.
This is another ورقي.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: كبيرة, plural: كبار).

examples.trans: We use this big paper ledger.
You know older brothers well!

meanings.note: Definite الليلة means 'tonight', while indefinite ليلة means 'one night / night of'.

examples.trans: I am going to sleep well tonight.
We booked the room for three nights.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun كل means 'every' (كل يوم 'every day'); before a definite noun it means 'all / the whole' (كل الأسبوع 'all week').

examples.trans: Tell me everything I need to know.
Everyone is happy in the courtyard today.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian form of شيء; combines in كل شي ('everything'), أي شي ('anything'), ولا شي ('nothing').

examples.trans: Everything is ready on the table.

examples.text: رن الجرس إذا احتجت أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian all-purpose word for 'all set, fine, spot-on!'.

examples.trans: Everything has to be spot-on!
Alright, I can remember the sentences.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: غرف.

examples.trans: We have eight comfortable rooms at the guesthouse.
Room four is ready and clean.

meanings.note: Female given name of the retired piano teacher.

examples.trans: We used the word سعاد.
This is another سعاد.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أجراس.

examples.trans: The gate bell rang twice.
Listen to the sound of the bell in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Verb رنّ means 'to ring' (for a bell, phone, or timer).

examples.trans: We used the word رنّ.
This is another رنّ.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: مرات.

examples.trans: The doorbell rang twice.
I read the letter three times.

كمان.gloss: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)

meanings.en: also; too; again (كمان مرة once more)
meanings.note: Everyday Levantine word for 'also, too, more' (كمان مرة 'one more time / again').

examples.text: التفكير السريع أنقذ الفطور كمان مرة!
examples.trans: Quick thinking saved breakfast once again!
And I missed you too.

meanings.note: Subject pronoun 'I' for any speaker.

examples.trans: I am Nour, the new receptionist.
I am Salma from the kitchen.

صار.gloss: to become; happen; be alright (ما بصير must not)

meanings.en: to become; happen; be alright (ما بصير must not)
meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بصير, بيصير).

examples.trans: You became one of us quickly!
Did the water upstairs turn cold?

meanings.note: Placed AFTER the adjective or verb it intensifies: تقيلة كتير ('very heavy'), شكرا كتير ('thank you very much').

examples.trans: The smell is so good!
This suitcase is very heavy today.

meanings.note: Polite offer opener بتحب ('would you like to...?'), from حبّ (to love/like).

examples.trans: We used the word حبّ.
This is another حبّ.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: رنات.

examples.trans: The doorbell gave a single ring.
I heard two quick rings from the buzzer.

meanings.note: Feminine Arabic word meaning 'double' or 'twofold', agreeing with رنة.

examples.trans: We used the word مزدوج.
This is another مزدوج.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: فاضية, plural: فاضيين).

examples.trans: Is room six vacant tonight?
The street outside the gate is completely empty.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أسابيع.

examples.trans: Next week I have time off.
We stayed at the guesthouse all week.

meanings.note: Active participle of إجا ('to come'): means 'on the way / arriving' (جايين 'they are coming') and after a time noun 'next' (الأسبوع الجاي 'next week').

examples.trans: The guests are coming down the stairs now.
We will see you next week!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بستنى, بيستنى).

examples.trans: Wait a moment, I have an idea!
The suitcase is still waiting for its owner.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word for 'want / need', inflected with pronoun suffixes: بدي (I want), بدك (you want), بده (he/it wants), بدها (she/it wants), بدنا (we want), بدكم (you pl. want), بدهم (they want).

examples.trans: I want to read the booking ledger.
Jam bread needs unsalted butter.

meanings.note: Common Arabic verb مدّد meaning 'to extend' a stay or deadline.

examples.trans: We used the word مدّد.
This is another مدّد.

meanings.note: Feminine Arabic noun إقامة meaning 'stay/residence' with Suad's ending.

examples.trans: We used the word إقامة.
This is another إقامة.

meanings.note: Marks location ('at, by') and with pronoun suffixes expresses possession: عندي ('I have'), عندك ('you have'), عندنا ('we have').

examples.trans: A taxi just stopped at the door.
I have a reservation under the name Suad.

meanings.note: Placed directly after a noun in Jordanian to mean 'extra' (قطع زيادة extra pieces, الدرج الزيادة the extra stairs).

examples.trans: I brought two extra chairs for the courtyard.
I put a little extra mint in the tea.

meanings.note: Everyday conditional word 'if' for real possibilities.

examples.text: رني الجرس إذا احتجتي أي شي.
examples.trans: Ring the bell if you need anything.

examples.text: إذا فتحنا الساحة الصبح، الجيران بيفرحوا.
examples.trans: If we open the courtyard in the morning, the neighbours will be delighted.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بقبل, بيقبل).

examples.trans: Will you accept staying on as our reception manager?
She accepted the invitation gladly.

meanings.note: Invariant spoken Levantine future marker placed before a subjunctive verb (without ب-).

examples.text: ضيفة غرفة أربعة رح تقعد كل الأسبوع.
examples.trans: Room four's guest will stay all week.

examples.text: تاني يوم ما رح يكون ممل!
examples.trans: The second day is not going to be boring!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بعزف, بيعزف).

examples.trans: I am still waiting for you to play the scale!

examples.text: الكبير كان يعزف بيانو كل جمعة.
examples.trans: The older boy used to play piano every Friday.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: جمع.

examples.trans: The family gathers every Friday at noon.
On Friday the street is quiet.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أوقات.

examples.trans: Old pipes take time to warm up.
You arrived right on time.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: Please have a glass of hot mint tea.
There is black tea and coffee at breakfast.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative preposition ('for us').

examples.trans: We used the word لـ.
This is another لـ.

meanings.note: Before a time noun, طول (tuul) means 'all ... long / throughout' (طول الليل all night long, طول الأسبوع all week).

examples.trans: The rain fell all night long.
Breakfast is free all week long.

meanings.note: Detached object carrier إيا- used when a verb already has a bound indirect object pronoun (-ك).

examples.trans: We used the word إيا.
This is another إيا.

meanings.note: Polite everyday Jordanian address for an adult woman or female guest.

examples.trans: Good morning, madam, please come in!
The room is booked under Madam Suad.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (بنكتب, بينكتب).

examples.trans: Your name will be written in the big ledger!
The address was written in clear handwriting.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أقلام.

examples.trans: I found my pen in the jacket pocket.
We write the names with a pencil.

meanings.note: Paired with قلم in قلم رصاص ('pencil').

examples.trans: We write bookings in pencil.
The name is written in pencil underneath.

meanings.note: Spoken Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (لهون 'to here', من هون 'from here').

examples.trans: Here we use this big ledger.
Stay right here a minute.

meanings.note: Female given name belonging to the café's morning baker.

examples.trans: We used the word سلمى.
This is another سلمى.

meanings.note: Male given name of the guesthouse owner.

examples.trans: We used the word مازن.
This is another مازن.

meanings.note: Plural Jordanian Arabic verb meaning 'to be thrilled' or 'have a wonderful time'.

examples.trans: We used the word انبسط.
This is another انبسط.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian word for both casual 'yes / yeah' and 'oh! / ah!' upon noticing something.

examples.trans: Oh, the door opened! Thank you.
Yes, eight rooms and eight keys.

meanings.note: Everyday preposition 'on, at, to'; before ال- it regularly contracts to عال- ('al- / 'a-).

examples.trans: Your glasses are on your forehead!
Say hello to Salma for me!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: أفكار.

examples.trans: I have a great idea for breakfast!
What do you think of this idea?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: سعاة.

examples.trans: The postman brought a thick envelope.
I handed the signature to the mail carrier.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: A postcard arrived in the morning.
The postman rang the bell.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine verb حطّ ('to put/place').

examples.trans: We used the word حطّ.
This is another حطّ.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بطاقات.

examples.trans: There is a paper tag on the suitcase.
I wrote my name on the card.

meanings.note: Nisba adjective from بريد (mail); بطاقة بريدية means 'postcard'.

examples.trans: We used the word بريدي.
This is another بريدي.

meanings.note: Feminine Arabic word meaning 'foreign', agreeing with بطاقة.

examples.trans: We used the word أجنبي.
This is another أجنبي.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: سميكة, plural: سماك).

examples.text: مين ترك هاد المغلف السميك هون؟
examples.trans: Who left this thick envelope here?
Thick stone walls hold the warmth.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: صناديق.

examples.trans: The screwdriver is inside the toolbox.
We moved four boxes out of the hallway.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian feminine noun. Plural: بوابات.

examples.trans: The courtyard gate is open for guests.
The taxi stopped outside the gate.

meanings.note: Masculine word derived from مساء ('evening'), meaning 'evening'.

examples.trans: We used the word مسائي.
This is another مسائي.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: أيام.

examples.trans: Today the weather is sunny and warm in Amman.
Have a happy, successful day!

meanings.note: Ubiquitous Jordanian/Levantine encourager ('come on! / let us...!').

examples.trans: Come on, let us bring the bag down into the light!
Let us go check out the room right now!

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian verb; spoken present adds the b- prefix (باخد, بياخد).

examples.trans: Someone took my suitcase by mistake!
Old buildings take time to warm up.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun. Plural: مكاتب.

examples.trans: The keys are on the reception desk.
The wooden desk under the window is wide.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian masculine noun.

examples.trans: The reception desk is beside the door.
Thank you for the warm welcome.

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian adjective (feminine: قريبة, plural: قراب).

examples.text: علمت بيانو ببيت قريب من هون.
examples.trans: I taught piano in a house near here.
We booked a table at a nearby restaurant.
